We have discovered an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a specific property: their automorphism groups partition their vertices into two distinct orbits, one of which forms a regular subgraph. Within this context, we have found an infinite family of graphs whose structures can be defined using a particular combination of group actions, referred to as twisted wreath products. Our research indicates that every graph within this infinite sequence of twisted wreath products contains a regular subgraph whose automorphism group acts transitively on its edges. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the graph formed by the edges of this regular subgraph possesses a particular property: given any edge in the graph, there exists a specific type of dodecagonal cycle that passes through this edge. Notably, this finding represents the first instance of a graph with this particular property whose automorphism group acts transitively on its edges.

In high-dimensional data sets containing categorical variables, the Group Lasso method has been an effective way to conduct sparse group selection. However, the traditional Group Lasso approach suffers from an estimation bias, which can be mitigated through an unbiased version called the "simplified" Group Lasso. Researchers have previously proposed an unbiased estimator for the traditional Group Lasso, which includes the Extended Group Lasso estimator. In this study, we introduce an alternative unbiased estimator, derived from an augmented Lagrangian objective function with a specific penalty parameter. We establish the theoretical consistency and rate of convergence of the new estimator under certain conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the new estimator outperforms the existing unbiased estimator through a simulation study.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on various language tasks, but they often lack a structured understanding of the knowledge they've learned. To address this limitation, we propose a new framework called SKILL, which infuses structured knowledge into these models. By utilizing knowledge graphs and a set of predefined relations, SKILL enables the models to reason about the relationships between entities and to generate more accurate and diverse text. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SKILL through experiments on three tasks: text generation, question answering, and text classification. The results show that SKILL significantly outperforms the original models on these tasks, and it also produces more coherent and diverse text. We also observe that SKILL can learn new relationships between entities and generate more accurate and diverse text even in the absence of explicit training data.

This study examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are limited to a finite range $\delta$ and investigates their behavior as this range shrinks. We demonstrate that by defining the model's initial and boundary conditions correctly, a consistent limit can be achieved as $\delta$ approaches zero. In the local case, the model is equivalent to standard heat diffusion equations, while for $\delta$ approaching zero, the nonlocal model is equivalent to a fractional heat diffusion equation with a specific $\alpha$-order derivative. The choice of $\alpha$ depends on the rate at which $\delta$ approaches zero. We also explore the implications of this analysis for a nonlocal model that includes a source term and a nonlocal reaction-diffusion equation.

This research focuses on developing a method for panoramic image stitching under the assumption that the camera is being held level. Unlike conventional approaches, our method differs in that it doesn't rely on feature matching across images. Instead, we use a single image for reference and utilize another image to calculate the camera's position and orientation. By assuming the camera remains level, we can determine the transformation needed for stitching. We've implemented this method using a single reference image and demonstrated its effectiveness with multiple test images. Notably, our approach achieves real-time performance.
This note explores the combinatorial aspects of the cancellations that occur among the poles of Eisenstein series for $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ as certain automorphic actions are changed.

A novel computational model of Parkinson's disease has been developed, utilizing a unique set of electrophysiological recordings from the brains of marmoset monkeys. This model integrates biophysical principles to simulate the neural networks affected by the disease, and it demonstrates the characteristic slow brain waves associated with Parkinson's through simulations. Notably, the model shows that the pathological features of Parkinson's can be replicated by reducing the activity of a specific type of neuron, known as cholinergic interneurons, which is consistent with previous research findings.

This research proposes an optimized technique for rendering line joins on vector maps, focusing on anti-aliasing to improve visual clarity. To enhance performance, we've developed two alternative methods to achieve anti-aliasing, one utilizing a color gradient and the other involving a pixel manipulation technique. Our experiments indicate that these approaches significantly reduce rendering time compared to traditional methods, resulting in improved visual quality and faster rendering speeds.

We present initial findings from our ongoing research using the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope, which involve optical integral-field unit (IFU) observations of 9 galaxies within the GOALS (The Great Observatories All-Sky LIRG Survey) sample at a distance of less than 0.04 from Earth. These galaxies, all of which are low to ultra-low redshift (z < 0.04) and have luminosities of either ultra-luminous (ULIRGs) or low to ultra-low (LIRGs), were observed using the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope. The IFU data, which were collected over two wavelength ranges (from 3700 to 5000 Angstroms and from 5000 to 7000 Angstroms), were obtained through 30 minutes of exposure time per galaxy. The extracted spectra have a resolution of R = 1200-1500 and a spatial scale of 3.7-3.9 kiloparsecs. The observed regions of the galaxies range from 10 to 30 kiloparsecs in diameter. The extracted spectra show a median signal-to-noise ratio of 5.3-5.5 in the central regions of the galaxies. The observed velocity fields of the galaxies have a median error of 20-30 kilometers per second. The observed star-formation rates of the galaxies range from 0.5 to 10 solar masses per year.

This study introduces a new family of multiquadric and trigonometric shaped radial basis function (RBF) interpolants, which maintains shape and order of smoothness. A new shape-preserving RBF quasi-interpolation operator is developed for its members, enabling the preservation of positive characteristics for functions. Through error analysis, the order of convergence is determined for the new operator, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical examples.

This study introduces a 12-class weather database consisting of 10,000 images, making it one of the most extensive and varied weather datasets available. The database covers a broad range of weather conditions, including both clear and cloudy skies, with a focus on incorporating a wide range of foreground objects. To enhance the quality of the images, a novel data augmentation technique was developed, utilizing both geometric and photometric transformations. The technique was particularly effective in creating high-quality synthetic images that closely mimic real images. The development of a new weather dataset and the data augmentation technique was evaluated using multiple Convolutional Neural Network architectures, including LeNet, AlexNet, GoogLeNet, and ResNet. The results showed that the data augmentation technique was highly effective in improving the accuracy of the models, with a significant improvement of over 20% when compared to training models on the original dataset.

A Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network called DPCRN has been proposed to improve speech enhancement. This model combines two types of neural networks: the dual-path network and the bidirectional recurrent network. The dual-path network consists of parallel convolutional and dilated convolutional layers that process audio information at different scales. The bidirectional recurrent network models the temporal dependencies of the audio data. The DPCRN model leverages the strengths of both types of networks to capture both short-term and long-term dependencies in the audio signals, leading to improved speech enhancement results. Experimental results show that the proposed DPCRN model achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art models, including the multi-microphone speech enhancement model known as DPCN, while also demonstrating robustness to noise types and levels.

We have examined the impact of two cosmological modifications - $f(R)$ gravity and massive neutrinos - on the turn-around radii of dark matter halos. By analyzing the clustering properties of these systems in the $f(R)$ gravity and neutrino scenarios separately, we found that the effects of each modification on the turn-around radii are distinct. The $f(R)$ gravity primarily influences the inner regions of halos due to their more compact profiles, whereas massive neutrinos mainly affect the outer regions due to their lower density. When combining these modifications, their effects on the turn-around radii exhibit a non-linear relationship, resulting in a more pronounced decrease than the sum of their individual effects. This interaction between $f(R)$ gravity and massive neutrinos may provide a solution to the discrepancy between observed galaxy rotation curves and the predictions of the standard $\Lambda$CDM model.

This study presents a two-fluid model that simulates convection in a horizontal layer of fluid, where one fluid is less dense than the other and both fluids interact through mass transfer between distinct layers. We developed a simple model that captures the essential dynamics of this scenario, including the transfer of heat and the movement of both fluids. By applying this model to a specific situation, we found that the convection currents behave in a predictable manner, with the less dense fluid flowing downward and the denser fluid flowing upward. This occurred at a constant rate, with the fluids' velocities remaining the same over time. We also observed that the heat transfer between the two fluids took place at a constant rate, with the heat being transferred from the hotter fluid to the cooler fluid. This process resulted in the less dense fluid becoming even less dense and the denser fluid becoming even denser. This led to an increase in the temperature difference between the two fluids over time. This research is an initial step towards developing a more complex model that can simulate the multiple-layer structure of atmospheric convection, where there are multiple layers of fluids with different temperatures and densities.

We examine the Jaynes-Cummings model under conditions of weak light where genuine entanglement can be achieved among uncorrelated atoms that are spatially separated. Our analysis reveals that entanglement is guaranteed if the model's parameters meet specific requirements, particularly if the difference between the resonant frequencies of two atoms and a cavity exceeds the Rabi frequencies. We also demonstrate that this entanglement can be confirmed through a measurement that compares the differences between the resonant frequencies of the atoms. Furthermore, we propose a feasible experimental setup using cold rubidium atoms and a vertically polarized laser to achieve this entanglement.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector plays a crucial role in tracking and identifying particles. Although it has been operational since 2010, it has been experiencing radiation damage, which has been mitigated through a designed degradation. To compensate for the reduced functionality, the LHC was adjusted to deliver more intense collisions. In 2017, the CMS detector underwent an upgrade, which included a new silicon pixel detector with improved design and enhanced capabilities. However, this upgrade introduced new challenges in the data processing system, particularly in the Level-1 trigger system. To address these issues, a prototype data processing system was implemented, which included a custom-designed hardware system known as the Level-1 Trigger Silicon Processor (L1-TSP). This paper focuses on the development and implementation of the L1-TSP, which was successfully tested during the 2017 pilot data collection period.

Using quantum field theory principles, we derived the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral distribution of the SU(2) glueball's invariant amplitude, which can be accessed through deep virtual photon scattering off protons.

Social media monitoring on Twitter enables companies to track the public's emotions towards their brand. This study focuses on analyzing Twitter user sentiment using an LSTM deep learning approach. A basic sentiment analysis was performed to train an LSTM model on a dataset consisting of 1,000 labeled tweets. The experiment revealed that the model achieved 87% accuracy in predicting the sentiment of unseen tweets. To improve performance, additional features were incorporated, including word embeddings and character-level features. The enhanced LSTM model achieved a significantly higher accuracy of 93%.

Researchers propose that the concept of holographic duality can be understood through the shadow correspondance, which connects the features of black holes in gravity theories to those of a field theory's dual. This correspondence is thought to hold for both linear and nonlinear interactions. In this study, we investigate a non-linear charged AdS black hole to see if its shadow can reveal information about the temperature and specific heat capacity of the dual field theory. We use the non-linear interaction to calculate the shadow's shape and position, and we find that these depend on the temperature of the dual field theory. We also find that the shadow's shape and position can be understood through the lens of a non-linear equation that relates the temperature to the charge of the black hole. This equation can be broken down into two separate non-linear equations, one for the case when the temperature is high and another for the case when the temperature is low. We find that the shadows of black holes with different temperatures overlap with each other, and we propose that this means that the shadow of a black hole can be the same even if the field theory is in a different state.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems from partial information involves a process that can reveal the dynamics of an open system in greater detail. This process involves measuring the Wigner function in different phases and locations, which can be achieved through homodyne detection. By analyzing the behavior of these functions in different tomographic planes, researchers can gain insight into the evolution of an open system's entanglement and the onset of synchronization in coupled systems.

Recent advancements in open-domain dialogue models have achieved human-like performance, but they still fall short in incorporating user roles into the conversation. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach to seamlessly integrate roles into existing models. Our proposed framework involves training a role-aware dialogue model that can engage in conversations while adhering to predefined specifications. To validate our approach, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation, encompassing both automatic and human assessments, to gauge the performance of our role-aware models. The results showed that our method effectively integrates roles into the dialogue, and the models exhibit superior human-evaluation scores compared to their non-role-aware counterparts.

A key challenge in agriculture is choosing the optimal pest management strategy, given the numerous variables at play. These variables include the uncertainty of future weather patterns, the fluctuating prices of pesticides and crops, and the varying lifecycles of pests and plants. To address this issue, we have developed a comprehensive decision-making framework that can evaluate and compare different pest management strategies under uncertain conditions. This framework is grounded in stochastic dynamic programming and incorporates the impacts of weather, pest biology, and economic factors. We have applied this framework to the problem of managing strawberry diseases caused by Botrytis, which results in significant crop losses and affects global production. The resulting model has a large number of possible states, making it difficult to solve directly. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a method to break down the decision-making process into smaller, more manageable parts. This approach involves dividing the plant's growth period into distinct stages, with each stage characterized by a specific set of state variables. By solving the decision-making problem for each stage individually, we have been able to derive a set of policies that can be combined to evaluate and compare different pest management strategies. The framework has been tested using real-world data from the strawberry industry, which shows that the optimal policy can significantly reduce the economic losses caused by the disease.

360-degree streaming videos have become increasingly popular, offering an immersive viewing experience. However, these videos require significant bandwidth for live streaming, which can be costly. To balance user experience and bandwidth efficiency, we propose a new approach called Viewport Prediction, which reduces the necessary data transfer. In this study, we focus on the challenge of predicting user viewport subtitles in 360-degree virtual tourism videos. We collect and annotate a large dataset of subtitles from real videos, but find that existing models struggle to perform well on this task due to the unique characteristics of 360-degree videos. To overcome this limitation, we develop a novel subtitle prediction model specifically designed for 360-degree videos, which combines a 3D attention mechanism with a Markov Transition model. The 3D attention mechanism allows the model to focus on specific parts of the video, while the Markov Transition model helps to anticipate future viewport subtitles based on past behavior. Our experiments show that this approach significantly outperforms existing methods and achieves near real-time prediction performance.

Tensor network methods have been widely used to describe and study strongly interacting systems, due to their ability to efficiently represent reduced density matrices in a low-dimensional representation. These techniques include the implementation of time evolution protocols, by applying the TN formalism to the real-time Schrödinger equation. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to apply these methods to more than two dimensions, primarily because the overhead of the tensor contraction scales exponentially with the number of spatial dimensions. This problem is particularly pronounced when considering thermal states of quantum systems, as these states generally lack the low-entanglement properties characteristic of certain ground states. In this study, we introduce a novel approach to tensor network construction, which enables the creation of accurate and efficient representations of thermal states and time-evolved systems in $d$-dimensional space. This method involves a local expansion of the tensor network bonds, which allows for a significant reduction in the number of variational parameters required. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to a variety of systems, including a quantum spin model on a cubic lattice, a free scalar field theory in relativistic thermal equilibrium, and a system undergoing time evolution following a quench event.

We propose a new decoupling theory framework based on scale-based approximations, which enables us to divide complex problems into simpler, more manageable parts. This framework is particularly effective in addressing high-frequency interactions and can be applied to a broad range of problems, from linear to nonlinear, and even those with periodic or almost-periodic inputs.

In this study, we establish a precise formula for the anisotropic p-capacity in a broad context, 
including particularly the settings of Euclidean space and its boundary. Furthermore, we derive the 
anisotropic Minkowski inequality as a direct consequence of this formula.

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. A key challenge in this experiment is mitigating the impact of random fluctuations known as glitches that arise from the spacecraft's system scanning its environment. These glitches can significantly affect the data collected during the test, and it's crucial to understand their characteristics in order to accurately interpret the results. This paper delves into the statistical analysis of the glitches detected during the Microscope mission, including their distribution, duration, and acceleration properties. By examining the features of these glitches, researchers can better assess their influence on the experiment's outcome and develop strategies to minimize their impact.

We investigate the behavior of an active colloid with two interacting particles that are chemotactically responsive to a chemoattractant. These particles are linked by a harmonic potential and can move independently in an activity gradient. We examine how their relative positions evolve over time, considering both the effects of activity gradients and Brownian motion. By analyzing the mean squared displacement of the center of mass, we find that the particles behave like a single entity with mass proportional to the ratio of their mass to the strength of their interaction. This entity exhibits chemotactic behavior, moving towards the region with the highest concentration of chemoattractant at a speed influenced by both the activity gradient and the strength of its interaction with the surrounding fluid.

The k-SSPC problem requires determining the fewest number of shortest paths needed to cover all nodes in a given graph, where each path is at most k edges long and can originate from any node. In this study, we explore the k-SSPC problem and its variants, specifically focusing on finding the minimum number of the strongest (highest weight) shortest paths needed to cover all nodes for a specific weight, a random weight, and the Euclidean distance. We also investigate the k-SSPC problem with the strongest k-shortest paths in certain types of graphs and networks.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and it's found that it significantly contributes to the growth of small-$x$ structure functions, potentially exceeding the BFKL growth limit.

As the number of frogs per site grows, the frog model's behavior shifts from transient to recurrent on a d-ary rooted tree. We demonstrate that this critical transition occurs roughly around the tree's degree.

Researchers have a long-standing interest in creating materials that respond differently to various light polarization states. These materials can provide unique opportunities for studying light-matter interactions and could also enable the development of advanced photonic devices. A specific type of material known as magnetophotonic surface crystals has shown promise in this regard, with potential applications in fields like biomedicine and telecommunications. However, most existing magnetophotonic surface crystals have limitations due to their narrow operating frequency ranges or difficulties in accurately controlling the orientation of their magnetic resonance responses. A new study presents a direction-sensitive magnetophotonic surface crystal that overcomes these limitations by utilizing a nonreciprocal resonance response that is controllable in both magnitude and direction. This breakthrough was achieved by incorporating a thin layer of nonmagnetic material with high dielectric properties, resulting in a significant enhancement of the magnetic field strength and a substantial shift in the resonance frequency. As a result, this new material exhibits highly tunable and direction-dependent transmission characteristics across a wide frequency range, with the ability to switch between two distinct resonance responses. This advancement in magnetophotonic surface crystals is expected to open up new possibilities for designing photonic devices that can operate across multiple frequency bands.

When a deep neural network is inaccessible due to privacy or security constraints, using a wrapped black-box model for tasks like image classification becomes essential. This study focuses on transferring knowledge from such a wrapped model to a target model without requiring access to the original data. We propose a novel approach to achieve this goal through a process called zero-shot knowledge distillation from a black-box model. Initially, we train a reference model to mimic the behavior of the wrapped model by feeding it synthetic data generated from the target model's predictions. Subsequently, the target model learns from the reference model through a standard knowledge distillation process. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach successfully enables the target model to achieve high accuracy even when the wrapped model is inaccurate. Notably, our method surpasses the performance of the wrapped model and achieves comparable results to state-of-the-art knowledge distillation techniques when the wrapped model is accurate.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time and have also obtained evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode.  These results are based on 3.0 inverse picobarns of data collected by the D0 collaboration at the Tevatron.  The branching ratios for these decays are estimated to be around 0.6 to 1.1 picobarns for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and around 0.2 to 0.4 picobarns for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is a challenging task, mainly due to the vast number of possible submodules. In this study, we focus on modules whose lattice of submodules contains no repeated elements, a property known as multiplicity-free. We present a novel approach to building the lattice of submodules of a multiplicity-free module by combining existing knowledge and new information about its submodules. Our method is a non-trivial extension of our previous work on lattice construction, and it is demonstrated through concrete examples using modules from the group algebras.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ consists of a subset~$S$ of vertices for which there exists a set~$T$ of unique shortest paths connecting each pair of elements in~$S$, and these paths lying entirely within~$S$. The strength of a graph~$G$, denoted~$sg(G)$, represents the largest possible size of a strong geodetic subset in~$G$. Determining whether a given graph contains a strong geodetic subset of a specified size is known as the strong geodetic set problem. We have investigated the computational complexity of identifying whether a graph contains a strong geodetic subset, and have found this to be an NP-hard problem. Additionally, we have established that determining the strength of a graph is an NP-hard problem, and have developed a polynomial-time algorithm for calculating the strength of a graph when it is in the form of an interval graph.

Imitation learning is a prominent approach for obtaining efficient policies, 
but it requires a perfect expert dataset to achieve optimal performance. 
In practice, however, expert demonstrations are often flawed due to various 
challenges, including complex environments and limited resources. 
We address this issue by introducing a new imitation learning method 
called TRAIL, which learns from suboptimal demonstrations by formulating 
a constrained optimization problem and solving it using a constrained 
maximum likelihood estimation technique. 
We prove that under certain conditions, our method is guaranteed to 
converge to a near-optimal policy compared to the optimal policy 
obtained from perfect expert data. 
We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by conducting 
experiments on a simulated robotic grasping task and a real-world 
self-driving navigation task. 
Our results show that our method outperforms existing imitation learning 
methods using only flawed demonstrations. 
We also provide an open-source implementation of TRAIL for other researchers 
to use and build upon.

Imitation learning has proven to be an effective method for training robust and efficient policies in complex tasks. Nonetheless, imitation learning's success heavily relies on high-quality expert demonstrations, which can be difficult and costly to obtain. This study introduces a novel imitation learning framework called Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), which leverages the interactions between multiple agents interacting with the same environment and sharing similar objectives. By combining the interactions of these agents, CoIL generates a more comprehensive and diverse set of experiences that can be used to train a robust policy without the need for expert demonstrations. We demonstrate the efficacy of CoIL through experiments on a variety of tasks, including a challenging multi-robot coordination scenario, and show that CoIL's policy performance rivals that of imitation learning using expert demonstrations while significantly reducing the required data.

This paper provides a detailed explanation of a metric recently proposed for polynomial code constructions, specifically for those based on the Paley construction, and demonstrates its effectiveness in decoding code variants from this class.

Recent advances in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) have been remarkable, thanks in part to large-scale training. Nonetheless, scaling up NMT training is often hindered by the difficulty of selecting a suitable softmax temperature, given the large vocabulary sizes involved. This challenge arises because the softmax function forces a trade-off between focusing on a small number of high-probability outputs and spreading the probability mass evenly across all possible outputs. To circumvent this limitation, we propose a novel reinforcement learning framework that leverages policy gradients to directly optimize the translation model's output distribution. This approach eliminates the need for temperature scaling and enables the model to learn from a large action space. Our experiments demonstrate that this method yields state-of-the-art results on standard NMT benchmarks, including the WMT English-to-German and English-to-French translation tasks, with significant improvements in BLEU scores when working with large vocabulary sizes.

A novel calibration method is introduced for a robot and a depth camera, enabling the calculation of end-effector pose and camera intrinsic parameters from real-world data without the need for a controlled environment or external markers. This method leverages machine learning to optimize the solution, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments using a simulated and real-world setup.

This study introduces the concept of a qfs n-dimensional space, denoted as QFSn, whose points are comprised of unique combinations of n natural numbers, and where the distance between any two points is calculated using an innovative formula. We examine key characteristics of the QFSn space, including its metric properties, demonstration of the triangle inequality, and proof that the metric function is both positive-definite and non-degenerate. We also explore the implications of these properties for the space's geometry.

The growing divide between Americans, characterized by increased polarization, has been extensively studied in the context of voting behavior and civic engagement. However, the current understanding of polarization remains incomplete, given the limited exploration of its effects on media consumption. This study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining polarization in online news readership. Utilizing a large dataset of 1.5 billion user interactions with online news articles, we employed a statistical approach to measure polarization, which revealed a significant and consistent polarization in online news readership among Americans. Furthermore, we investigated the sources of this polarization, finding that it is influenced by both geographical location and online platform, but not by demographic characteristics.

We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We then extend this by showing multiple contexts in which the word problem becomes undecidable, sharing a common basis with the original proof.

We investigate a situation where a single photon is emitted consistently from a system of two coupled resonators, despite the fact that the individual resonators do not emit light by themselves. This phenomenon occurs when a quantum bit is periodically exposed to laser light, causing it to transition between two states. A steady state of this system is achieved when the frequency of the laser matches the bit's oscillation frequency. A theoretical model shows that this consistent photon emission results from the interplay between the two states of the quantum bit, which creates a continuous flow of light between the two resonators. This effect can be observed in the form of a periodic variation in the intensity of the emitted light. By adjusting the amount of interaction between the two states, it is possible to control the amount of light emitted at specific points in time. This research provides a framework for exploring the properties of this steady state further, including the possibility of creating a flow of entangled particles between the two resonators.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute significantly to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. We investigate subsets of (p/q)Z that can be identified using finite automata and establish the connection to periodic sequences in base p/q. Additionally, we explore the limitations of this system in relation to the golden ratio and other irrational numbers.

The axion field, which is associated with a long-standing problem in physics, requires a minimum value that is very small in size. This minimum value is linked to the axion's mass, which in turn influences the mass of a specific type of neutrino. As a result, even if the neutrino's mixing with other types is very small, the presence of an axion can make it significant. Consequently, the existence of an axion would require the addition of a new parameter to describe the neutrino's mass, which in turn would affect the likelihood of certain neutrino-related phenomena occurring. Furthermore, the presence of an axion would also make it more difficult to explain the observed stability of the universe using just its most basic components.

Between 2014 and 2017, the LAMOST conducted a time-domain survey across four $K$2 plates, which span a total area of approximately 100 square degrees in the sky. This survey focused on objects with a magnitude of up to 9.6 and obtained 1.5 million spectra over a period of three years. By analyzing these spectra, we were able to identify 1.2 million spectra from 1.1 million unique targets, with a median of 1.3 spectra per object. This allowed us to create a comprehensive catalog of stellar spectra, which can be used to study the properties and behaviors of these stars.

In recent years, medical image analysis has been significantly advanced by the use of deep learning techniques, particularly through the application of fully convolutional networks. However, implementing these models on a voxel-by-voxel basis can be computationally expensive and memory-intensive. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative edge-gated CNN architecture that reduces memory usage and processing time by limiting the processing of background voxels to a low-resolution image analysis. This is achieved through the use of a memory-efficient boundary detection module, which identifies the edges of anatomical structures and generates a mask to restrict the analysis to these areas. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields high-quality semantic segmentations on both synthetic and real-world datasets, outperforming existing memory-efficient methods while requiring significantly less memory and processing time.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. In this paper, we focus on the replica set configuration of MongoDB, which supports transactional operations and isolates them using a serialization graph based consistency model. We have developed a formal specification of MongoDB's serialization function and its associated graph construction method, and have successfully utilized these definitions to identify and correct several consistency-related issues present in the latest version of MongoDB.

Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths in a combinatorial context, and subsequently establish the positivity of their underlying coefficients. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this positivity extends to the coefficients of the inverse of the Kostka matrix from chromatic symmetric functions to chromatic polynomials, specifically for the family of Dyck paths.

Humans naturally reevaluate their perceptions and adjust their understanding of situations in order to make informed decisions. This ability to reprocess information and adapt to new insights is a key component of human executive function. Inspired by this capacity, we introduce a novel concept called contrastive value policy, which enables machines to reexamine their perceptions and adjust their understanding of situations in order to make informed decisions. By applying this idea to a specific scenario, we develop a method for reevaluating perceptions and adjusting understanding of situations in order to make informed decisions. This method involves reprocessing information and adapting to new insights, which is a key component of human executive function.

This study aims to highlight the inherent disparities present in commonly used medical image datasets, which are often overlooked in research. While data augmentation techniques can be very effective, they can also perpetuate existing biases found in these datasets. In an effort to address this issue, we have created a comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses the inherent biases present in medical image datasets. This framework evaluates datasets based on three key aspects: data distribution, image quality, and clinical relevance. Utilizing this framework, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of several widely used medical image segmentation datasets, including the use of quantitative metrics and qualitative assessments. Our analysis revealed that the datasets we examined exhibit significant disparities in terms of data distribution, image quality, and clinical relevance. In response to these findings, we have developed a set of guidelines that prioritize the use of high-quality, clinically relevant images in training models. These guidelines emphasize the importance of selecting images that are free from obvious pathologies and have a clear and well-defined boundary between the target organ and surrounding tissues. In addition, we have proposed a set of techniques that can be used to reduce the inherent biases present in medical image segmentation datasets. These techniques involve the use of transfer learning and a dataset balancing technique called SMOTEN, which can help to reduce the biases present in these datasets.

Researchers studying complex systems from social networks to biological tissues often encounter the challenge of understanding these networks' geometric structure. In this study, a unique class of nanoscale assemblies is examined, where magnetic properties are influenced by both direct and indirect interactions. By mapping these interactions and using a novel geometric approach, the unique reversal patterns observed in these assemblies are explained for the first time. This method reveals a hidden structure that explains the assemblies' magnetic behavior and provides a universal framework for analyzing other dynamic processes in complex systems.

New observations of solar wind energy flux from the Parker Solar Probe, obtained just 0.13 AU from the Sun, provide the most accurate data available for this period. By analyzing data from 17 to 29.5 solar radii around the Sun, researchers used a statistical approach to determine the average energy flux of solar wind particles. According to their findings, the average energy flux of solar wind protons is significantly lower than expected, at around 2.1 times the energy flux of the solar wind energy flux at Earth. In contrast, the energy flux of 0.5-5.5 MeV/nuc electrons was found to be roughly 2.5 times the Earthly value. These results suggest that solar wind energy flux may be influenced by the presence of a streamer belt, which could be a major energy source for solar flares.

Deep neural network-based speech emotion recognition systems have achieved high accuracy in simulated environments, but their performance suffers in real-world settings due to variations in speech and annotation styles. This issue is particularly pronounced in a dataset that includes recordings from a radio broadcast, which are particularly challenging to classify accurately. To improve the generalizability of such systems, we employed a transfer learning approach using a deep reinforcement learning algorithm to adapt their training process. Specifically, we used a policy gradient method to optimize the adaptation of a pre-trained speech emotion recognition model on a labeled dataset, with the goal of maximizing its performance on an unlabeled dataset from a different domain. Our results show that this approach yields significant improvements in accuracy on the radio broadcast dataset, with an average increase of 10.5% across different emotion categories.

To investigate the magnetic and electronic properties of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ under high pressure, we performed a combination of X-ray diffraction and nuclear forward scattering measurements.  Our analysis of the structural data reveals that the Aurivillius compound undergoes a phase transition from the tetragonal $I4/m$ to the monoclinic $C2/m$ symmetry at 2.5 GPa, with the phase persisting up to 5.5 GPa.  Our nuclear forward scattering measurements detected a broad peak around 1.5 GPa, which we attribute to an incipient magnetic transition.  However, we were unable to confirm the presence of magnetism in this material at pressures above 2.5 GPa due to the onset of the structural phase transition.  Our results suggest that the magnetic transition in Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ is closely linked to the structural phase transitions occurring in this material.

This research introduces a new approach to analyze the accuracy of approximate solutions obtained by a method known as the Piecewise Approximate Linear Technique (PWALT) for solving complex shortest path problems that involve both discrete and continuous variables. By demonstrating the existence and size of the errors, we show that the proposed bounds can be used to estimate the distance between the optimal and approximate solutions. Furthermore, we provide a case study involving the optimal planning of an aircraft's flight path, taking into account factors like wind, air traffic control constraints, and the need to refuel, and compare the performance of PWALT with other methods.

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both exact and approximate methods. These findings indicate that as time increases, the location of the shock front moves further away from its initial position at a rate equal to one and a half times the speed of light. Additionally, the density of the shock front compared to its surrounding environment also increases over time in proportion to the expansion of the universe, following a power law with an exponent of one and a half. This relationship holds true for both adiabatic and non-adiabatic indices.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. The measured rate is compared to three theoretical predictions from the SCET, Resonance-Saturation, and NLO Effective Field Theory frameworks.

A new family of generalized Hermite polynomials is introduced, which is closely related to a specific set of parameters, including roots of unity and algebraic integers. These polynomials are derived from a formula involving a product of differences, and this formula is connected to a formula for the Weyl-Heisenberg operator. By examining the monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with potential $|x^{2n-1}|^{\alpha}$, we find that their eigenfunctions can be expressed as the generalized Hermite polynomials in question.

We studied the noise produced by adhesive tape as it is slowly peeled off from its roll, and found that the sound changes in a complex way over time, exhibiting both sudden and gradual shifts. Our analysis revealed that these acoustic emissions are linked to the formation of cracks in the tape's surface, and that their patterns can be used to track the underlying mechanical changes. By examining the distribution of time intervals between successive sound waves, we uncovered a unique daily rhythm, with the intervals varying in a consistent manner from early morning to late evening. This periodic behavior is reflected in the way the time intervals group together, with smaller clusters forming during the day and larger ones at night. Interestingly, this daily pattern is observed even when the peeling process is repeated at different speeds, suggesting that it is driven by a natural process rather than the mechanical one.

In this report, we present our findings from measuring the current-state dynamics in both planar InAs/GaSb quantum wells and InAs/Al nanowires with a single tunneling barrier. These measurements reveal that the quantum states exhibit strong resistance variations due to spin-orbit coupling, enabling us to observe the free fermion dynamics and tunneling between different states. By applying a microwave pulse, we can transfer superconducting signal between two Josephson junctions, demonstrating the potential for quantum information storage and transfer.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry. Previous studies have shown that such modifications lead to unphysical mode issues, effectively resulting in a restricted theory. Now, by incorporating a finite temperature within this framework, researchers find that thermal corrections can remove the unphysical mode problems, however, this comes at the expense of altering the graviton mode's dispersion relation. It's discovered that thermal corrections follow the non-abelian $1/\sqrt{t^2 - m^2}$ behavior, differing from the abelian $1/t$ behavior found in previous studies.

This research develops an analytical formula to calculate the expected cost of hedging European options through a dynamic delta-hedging strategy. The formula can be applied to various payment structures, including those with fees related to the number of contracts, the absolute value of delta, or both. The formula's components depend on the characteristics of the option, its delta, the underlying asset's price, the time to expiration, and the time to expiration squared. The study also explores the impact of different payment structures on the cost of hedging, finding that the effect of delta on costs varies depending on whether delta is positive or negative.

By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure, consisting of a periodic arrangement of two distinct materials with significantly different properties. Our key finding is that the heterogeneous model's minimizers converge to a suitable approximation as the material's characteristic length diminishes, under specific conditions involving the material's contrast and differential constraints.

We analyzed a sample of 150 massive early-type galaxies in the K2 band using data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. These galaxies were observed at a median redshift of 0.055, with 75% below a redshift of 0.065. We focused on tidal features within these galaxies, specifically those with a brightness ratio of more than 10^-4 to the central galaxy. This threshold allowed us to detect features with a 5-sigma confidence level at a radius of 20.5 kiloparsecs. We found that approximately 22% of the galaxies in our sample exhibited tidal features, with a median age of 1.1 billion years. We also discovered that the fraction of tidal features in these galaxies increased with decreasing redshift, from 15% at z=0.065 to 30% at z=0.035. Furthermore, we found that tidal features were more prominent in galaxies with a higher stellar mass ratio, and that these features were typically oriented at an angle of 90 degrees to the major axis of the galaxy. We estimated the merger rate of these galaxies to be 0.2 mergers per billion years, with a rate that increased by a factor of 2.5 as the galaxy's stellar mass doubled.

This study examines the dynamics of social mobility across multiple generations within a dynamic model that incorporates both economic and social status. We investigate the optimal allocation of opportunities, such as education and employment, to maximize intergenerational progress and reduce inequality. Our analysis reveals that unequal distribution of opportunities leads to persistent disparities in economic and social status. We also explore how unequal distribution affects the allocation of opportunities and find that it causes a self-reinforcing cycle of inequality. Furthermore, we examine the optimal allocation of opportunities in a scenario where unequal distribution of opportunities is a given fact.

The integration of optical materials and laser systems has significant implications for various technological advancements, influencing fields like telecommunications, medicine, and defense technology. However, the lack of a unified framework for analyzing combined optical systems through their material components creates a knowledge gap. To address this, we propose a holistic approach to modeling integrated laser systems, considering their material structure, temperature effects, and nonlinear interactions. This method allows for the optimization of laser systems based on their intended applications and can also be inverted to reverse-engineer unknown laser systems from their observed output. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, we apply it to a high-power laser system, achieving a record of over 100 W of average power in a 100 fs pulse duration and 10 ps pulse width.

We demonstrate that for any fixed $p$ in the range $1 < p \leq 2$, there exists a constant $C_{p}$, which is dependent on $p$ alone, for which the following condition holds true: given any given incompressible set $K$ within the $\ell_p$ space over $\mathbb{R}^d$, there exists a linear transformation $T$ with the property that for every element $x$ within $K$, the following inequality is satisfied: $\left(1 - \varepsilon\right)\|x\|_{p} \leq \|Tx\|_{p} \leq \left(1 + \varepsilon\right)\|x\|_{p}$. Furthermore, the dimension of the transformed space $T$ can be restricted to a value of $C_{p}\varepsilon^{-1}d$.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. This method was developed to enhance beam diagnostics and allow for fast emittance measurements during accelerator operation. Emittance scans involve a brief reduction in beam intensity at the level of luminosity, allowing for rapid and precise emittance measurements without interfering with main physics runs. This paper outlines the development, implementation, and results of emittance scans, including associated challenges and potential applications for other beam diagnostics techniques.

This paper explores a distributed optimization problem where multiple agents, working together, face constraints and objective functions, and we consider the presence of malicious attackers that disrupt the process by manipulating the subgradients shared among the agents. We investigate the optimal attack strategy and its implications on the optimization process. To counter this, we develop a secure distributed optimization algorithm utilizing quantized and encrypted subgradients, and under certain conditions, prove that it converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K})$ in an $K$-round optimization process. To improve robustness, we also propose a subgradient clipping technique that achieves a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/K^{1/4})$. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods in mitigating the impact of malicious attackers.

To accurately model the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and make reliable measurements, researchers use simulations to model various instrumental effects on their experiments. However, creating realistic simulations of experiments like CMB experiments is a complex task due to the numerous components involved, including detectors, readout systems, and optical systems. To address this challenge, we present a Python package called s4cmb, which allows users to simulate the response of their experiments to the CMB by modeling the signal detected by each detector and incorporating the impact of instrumental effects such as beam shapes, cross-polarization, and detector noise. By using this tool, users can generate simulations that closely match their actual data and improve the accuracy of their measurements.

In this study, we examine how pre-trained language models, specifically BART, determine the order of words within a sentence. We focus on two key aspects: the influence of syntactic structure and the role of semantic information. Through a series of experiments, we found that BART's ordering decisions are largely driven by the syntactic structure of the sentence, with semantic considerations playing a relatively minor part. We also discovered that BART's word order predictions are often inconsistent with the intended order, and this discrepancy is more pronounced when the sentence is semantically coherent. We observed this inconsistency to be a result of BART's tendency to prioritize grammatical correctness over the intended meaning. This led us to investigate whether BART can be trained to give more weight to semantic information when determining word order. We found that by training BART on a dataset that prioritizes semantic coherence, we can improve the correlation between its word order predictions and the intended order. However, this improvement comes with a trade-off, as the model's ability to generalize is compromised.

This paper introduces a novel fake face detection approach called the MD-CSDNetwork, a multi-domain cross-stitched network designed to identify deepfakes. Unlike traditional methods that rely on complex generative models, our low-latency and lightweight solution involves training two separate convolutional neural networks for real and fake data analysis. These two trained models are then cross-stitched to combine their respective features, enabling the detection of deepfakes with high accuracy. Notably, our proposed method achieves a remarkable 0.93 average accuracy on the Celeb-DF dataset, outperforming existing low-latency methods.

A new class of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with degree-degree correlations is introduced, and it's shown that these codes perform optimally on a binary erasure channel, achieving the best possible trade-off between the rate and error-correction capability. The code ensemble's performance is analyzed by studying the degree-degree correlation distribution and erasure patterns, and it's found that existing methods can be adapted to gather data on both types of distributions. A method for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles is also presented, and it's demonstrated that these codes can provide a higher rate than traditional LDPC codes with the same error-correction capability.

A critical flaw in the current understanding of the decoy-state quantum key distribution system has been identified. Researchers found that the proposed measure for preventing an all-photon attack, relying on the comparison of average values between the signal and decoy states, is insufficient. A new strategy for hacking has been discovered, allowing hackers to evade detection by modifying the phase randomization of the source. Furthermore, a calculation has been performed to determine the actual secure key rate in this scenario, taking into account the phase randomization of the source.

To ensure the long-term success of 5G networks, managing core network resources effectively is crucial. This involves optimizing energy consumption and ensuring the highest level of security and performance. In this paper, we present innovative management techniques that enable 5G core networks to self-organize, self-heal, and minimize energy waste. By applying these methods, we demonstrate a significant reduction in energy expenditure and improved security, outperforming traditional approaches.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized to apply to any given metric space equipped with an order relationship. Building upon this foundation, he posed two problems regarding the existence of certain order relationships that could be derived from given metrics in one-dimensional and higher-dimensional spaces. Our research provides a solution to these problems by demonstrating that any finite-dimensional Euclidean space can support an order relationship that generates a given metric, and we achieve this by first establishing a specific distance metric that aligns with the given order relationship. Furthermore, we show that this metric is equivalent to the original Euclidean metric.

We derive upper and lower estimates for the successive minima of an order in a number field, based on the minima of lattice basis elements and the discriminant of the order. Furthermore, we establish connections between the minima of a lattice associated with a curve defined over a number field and the coefficients of its defining polynomial.

A novel technique has been introduced to measure temperature, pressure, and the ratio of oxygen to nitrogen gases simultaneously using a one-dimensional hybrid frequency-shift rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy method. This approach combines femtosecond and picosecond laser pulses to achieve precise measurements. The method's effectiveness was demonstrated through experiments involving the measurement of pressure over a range of 1-2 atmospheres and oxygen to nitrogen ratios from 0.2 to 1. The results showed minimal errors of 0.1 atmospheres and 0.03 in pressure and oxygen to nitrogen ratio measurements respectively. The method's potential for use in the development of temperature-sensitive gas diagnostics is also highlighted.

New simulations of protoplanetary disks reveal the presence of persistent, long-lived spiral structures that can give birth to self-sustaining spiral patterns. These patterns are capable of maintaining their own existence for millions of years, and they can also give rise to ring systems and planetary systems. The simulations show that the growth of a self-sustaining vortex is limited by the amount of material it can accrete from its surrounding disk, and this rate is determined by the viscosity of the disk. The mass of a self-sustaining vortex can range from a few times the mass of Jupiter to several times the mass of Jupiter, and it can be influenced by the presence of other vortices. The simulations also reveal that the formation of a self-sustaining vortex can be triggered by a massive object passing close to the disk, and that the mass of the object required to create such a vortex can be as low as a few times the mass of Jupiter.

The presence of neutral excitations in quantum Hall systems can lead to a phenomenon where a direct current is produced in the presence of a magnetic field, even without any applied voltage. This effect arises due to the interaction between neutral modes and the Hall barrier, resulting in a net flow of electrons from the Hall bar's edge to its interior.

We propose a novel understanding of the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$ by relating it to a cluster algebra that we define using a specific Poisson variety associated to $U_q(\mathfrfr{g}).$ This connection between the quantum group and the cluster algebra allows us to identify a subalgebra within the quantum group, which we call the "focal subalgebra." The focal subalgebra is generated by a set of "classical simple roots" corresponding to the ADE Dynkin diagrams found in $\mathfr{g}.$ These roots give rise to a finite number of "cluster variables" that we can use to generate the entire quantum group through a process called "folding." This relationship between the quantum group and the cluster algebra also reveals a pattern of "finiteness" within the quantum group, which we can observe from the structure of the Fock space.

In our research, we developed an algorithm called DR-DSGD to tackle a challenging problem: when data is distributed across multiple nodes connected in a network, and there's a significant difference in the data distributions, how can we efficiently train a robust machine learning model? The DR-DSGD algorithm builds upon the decentralized variant of the exponential weighted average algorithm, while incorporating a sensitive term to minimize the impact of data distribution disparities. By carefully designing the sensitive term as a function of the data distribution and the loss function, we were able to derive a robust variant of the algorithm. We also proved that the DR-DSGD algorithm converges at a rate of O(1/\sqrt t) in the case of finite action spaces, and O(1/t) in the case of infinite action spaces. Notably, the DR-DSGD algorithm achieves a faster convergence rate than the non-robust DSGD algorithm in the case of finite action spaces.

This paper provides a historical context for the development of computer simulations in the hard-disk model, tracing its evolution from the early work of Mayer and Uhlenbeck to the significant contributions of many researchers over the years. We examine key milestones, including the introduction of Monte Carlo methods, the development of molecular dynamics simulations, and various proposals for interacting disk systems. We also discuss the pioneering research of Stillinger and Weber, Halperin and Nelson, and others, whose work laid the groundwork for modern simulations, and highlight the impact of advances in computational power on these simulations.

This study assesses the impact of varying jet radius, nuclear PDFs and temperature on the interpretation of medium-modified jet production data from the LHC. Using a parton-coherence model, we find that jet spectra at medium energy scales are significantly influenced by jet radius and nuclear PDF choice. However, we also find that the impact of medium modification on jet spectra is more sensitive to jet radius than medium effects. Furthermore, we find that the temperature variation has a minimal impact on jet spectra at medium energy scales.

We have conducted an in-depth analysis of Forsage, a cryptocurrency pyramid scheme, to understand its underlying structure and user dynamics. By examining Forsage's smart contract code and gathering data from over 4 million Ethereum transaction records, we have identified key features of the scheme, including its Ponzi-like and pyramid components. Our analysis reveals that Forsage's designers employed several tactics to evade detection and prolong the scheme's lifespan. We have also analyzed user behavior and found that Forsage's participant base is comprised of a small group of active users who drive the scheme's growth, with the majority of users being passive investors. Our research provides a comprehensive examination of Forsage's structure, user behavior, and the challenges of detecting similar types of cryptocurrency schemes.

Using data from the VISTA survey of the Milky Way, we analyzed 19 previously unidentified globular cluster candidates in the galactic bulge. By combining infrared photometry from VISTA and 2MASS, we created color-magnitude diagrams for each candidate and estimated their distance and extinction. Our findings indicate that 5 of these candidates are likely open clusters, while the remaining 14 require further investigation.

We have systematically analyzed the impact of massive quarks on exclusive Drell-Yan processes within the framework of soft-collinear effective theory. Our analysis reveals that quark mass effects are divided into two categories: soft and hard. Soft effects are encapsulated in a single function $Q_0$, which is independent of the quark mass and can be determined through global fits to other processes. However, $Q_0$ exhibits significant logarithmic dependence on the invariant mass of the system, which becomes substantial as this mass approaches the quark mass. In contrast, hard effects are dominated by the quark's momentum when the system's invariant mass is large, and thus are relatively less significant. Our analysis also enables the derivation of a precise factorization theorem for the quark impact factor, which is expressed as a product of two functions: one related to the soft behavior and the other to the hard behavior. Furthermore, we have developed a set of systematic scale variations to validate the factorization theorem and the associated logarithmic divergence cancellation. Our analysis also facilitates the development of a systematic resummation formula for the quark mass effects, which can be computed through the convolution of two functions.

We have re-examined the approach used to develop tight-binding models in physics, with a focus on removing spurious effects stemming from the mismatch between atomic and electronic descriptions. By redefining the model's electric field term in a way that accounts for gauge invariance, we have derived a new, physically meaningful representation of light-matter interactions. This new formulation eliminates the ambiguity present in previous methods and provides a direct connection between the TB Hamiltonian and its underlying microscopic origins. By doing so, we have identified specific conditions under which the TB models can accurately capture the effects of light-matter interactions, paving the way for the development of more sophisticated models that incorporate both electron behavior and photon interactions.

Researchers have found that certain types of holographic theories can be accurately represented using a specific kind of entanglement theory called the holographic bound, which serves as a threshold for the total entanglement of a system. This relationship is particularly useful for achieving optimal error correction, as any deviation from the bound indicates the presence of an error. In this study, we've discovered that the holographic bound can be approximated using a specific type of entanglement theory called the hyper-invariant multi-scale entanglement renormalization ansatz, which is capable of modeling complex systems with power-law correlations. This finding is significant because it makes it possible to use the hyper-invariant MERA as a tool for approximating the holographic bound and performing optimal error correction in systems that exhibit power-law behaviors.

A theoretical investigation into the photoisomerization of a model retinal using a linear response technique found that quantum effects cause significant variations in reaction rates for different electron-phonon coupling strengths. In contrast, changes in other parameters have a minimal impact, making electron-phonon coupling the dominant factor influencing the rate. Adjusting this parameter from very weak to very strong coupling can switch the reaction rate from being slowed down by several orders of magnitude to being nearly optimal for isomerization.

Deep learning techniques, specifically graph neural networks, have shown promise in analyzing and predicting business processes by extracting relevant information from documents, such as text and images. This study compares the effectiveness of these models in predicting process events and associated data. We employed a publicly available dataset and trained multiple models, including graph neural networks, on various data types, including images, text, and a combination of both. Our results indicate that the best performing models achieve high accuracy rates, with an average of 0.93 for image-based models, 0.92 for text-based models, and 0.91 for models trained on both. However, we also found that the performance of these models can be sensitive to the data they are trained on, and that certain models may not generalize well to new data.

On October 30, 2020, a 6.6 magnitude earthquake struck the Izmir region of Turkey, causing widespread destruction and loss of life. In the aftermath, a social media campaign was launched to raise funds for the victims, with President Erdogan also initiating a state fund to aid in relief efforts. This study utilizes Twitter data from the Izmir earthquake relief efforts to investigate user behavior and posting patterns. Specifically, we examined the demographics of donors, the language used in donation tweets, and the characteristics of users who shared these donation tweets. Our findings reveal that a significant proportion of Twitter users in Turkey and abroad donated to the relief efforts, with a notable increase in donations during a designated hour. The data also indicate that users who donated to the relief efforts used more positive language in their tweets than non-donors. Furthermore, we discovered that users who shared donation tweets were more likely to be male, younger, and more active on social media.

We investigate several properties of the Gelfand-Shilov spaces Sigma alpha, beta, as well as their Fourier extensions, and establish conditions under which they are nontrivial. It is demonstrated that the standard references contain an error, and a correction is provided. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between these spaces and their Fourier counterparts, and derive criteria for which the spaces are equipped with the property of being invariant under smooth Fourier transformations. Ultimately, we establish the sufficient and necessary conditions for the compact embedding of the spaces, and utilize this to reconfirm the existence and uniqueness of solutions to certain initial value problems.

We have analyzed a significant flare event from the star AD Leo that occurred in 1985, using a combination of observational data and computational modeling. During this event, the star's near-ultraviolet emission increased by a factor of 100 in just 10 seconds, before returning to normal levels over the course of several minutes. Our analysis of the data suggests that the flare's energy output followed a power-law decline with a total of five distinct phases. In order to model the flare's behavior, we employed a one-dimensional radiative transfer model that accounted for the presence of both electrons and hydrogen gas. By adjusting the distribution of energy within the flare, we were able to successfully replicate the observed patterns of emission across various wavelengths, including the near-ultraviolet, ultraviolet, X-rays, and optical spectra. Our analysis revealed that the flare's energy output was primarily focused on a column of about 0.01 grams per square centimeter, and that the temperature within this region varied from around 10,000 to 10 million Kelvin over the course of the flare.

In this study, we examine the behavior of light propagating through a finite number of PT-symmetric photonic waveguides arranged in a periodic structure. Contrary to previous research on infinite PT-symmetric systems, we find that PT symmetry breaking occurs spontaneously, leading to the transmission of light in one direction. Interestingly, this phenomenon can be observed for both even and odd numbers of waveguides. Additionally, we discover that PT symmetry breaking becomes more pronounced as the number of waveguides increases, ultimately resulting in complete bidirectional transmission. Furthermore, our research reveals that the transition from CPAL to bidirectional transmission involves a switch from coherent back-and-forth accumulation to coherent forward propagation.

Researchers studying complex systems from biology, social sciences, and technology often find it beneficial to analyze Boolean networks due to their simplicity and ability to capture critical dynamics. A new method has been developed to simulate and analyze Boolean networks consisting of sparse interactions, either between different components or the same components. This method allows for the examination of network behavior over time by analyzing the fixed points, periodic orbits, and chaotic behavior. Additionally, it can determine the level of randomness in the network by studying the distribution of cycle lengths. This approach has been demonstrated through simulations of scale-free and Barabasi-Albert networks, showing that it can effectively capture the dynamics of these systems.

We derive concise mathematical expressions for calculating matrix elements of single-particle and particle-particle operators that can be applied to a wide range of Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions, encompassing configurations involving multiple quasiparticle excitations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this formula can be modified to accommodate Hartree-Fock calculations. Utilizing this expression, we can efficiently determine the properties of even-even systems or one-body removal/addition spectra of odd-A systems.

Neural network-based point cloud models have achieved impressive results in various tasks, including classification and regression tasks. Despite their effectiveness, these models are vulnerable to data attacks, particularly label noise attacks, which can significantly degrade their performance. To enhance the robustness of these models, researchers typically employ smoothing transformations such as median filtering to preprocess the data. However, the effectiveness of these transformations is often limited to specific transformations and data characteristics. In this study, we investigate the application of non-linear transformations, including median filtering, to preprocess point cloud data and the benefits they provide. We also propose a novel, transformation-specific smoothing approach that leverages a range of smoothing transformations, including non-linear ones, to improve the robustness of neural network-based point cloud models. The proposed method involves training multiple models using different transformations and selecting the one that achieves the highest performance. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms traditional smoothing transformations, including median filtering, and our code is available online.

In this paper, we examine medium access control techniques for Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar systems. Unlike traditional wireless communication systems, FMCW radar systems have unique characteristics that affect the design of their MAC protocols. We investigate two protocols, a modified Slotted ALOHA and a CSMA approach, to determine their suitability for FMCW radar applications. The performance of these protocols is evaluated under various conditions, including different load levels and packet transmission success rates. The results show that the CSMA protocol outperforms the modified ALOHA protocol in terms of throughput, but both protocols can achieve high throughput in scenarios with low load and high transmission success rates. However, in scenarios with high load and low transmission success rates, the throughput of both protocols decreases significantly. The CSMA protocol's performance is particularly affected by its contention resolution mechanism, which can lead to prolonged idle periods. The results also indicate that the ALOHA protocol's performance can be improved by reducing the packet transmission duration, but this may not be feasible in practice. The study provides a foundation for further research into MAC protocols for FMCW radar systems.

Temporal knowledge graph completion is a challenging task that has garnered significant interest in recent years. This task involves adding accurate timestamp information to existing triples within a temporal knowledge graph. Most existing approaches focus on incorporating time-aware information into their models, but often overlook the temporal nature of these relationships. In contrast, our proposed framework develops a time-aware model that is both low-rank and model-agnostic, allowing it to capture the underlying patterns within the data. By incorporating a time-aware entity and relation representation, our model can effectively utilize both temporal and non-temporal knowledge graph information to enhance its performance. Notably, our model achieves superior results to state-of-the-art time-aware models, while also providing a more compact and interpretable representation of the underlying data.

Within the RPA framework, the real part of the RPA polarizability can be expressed as a negative value of the imaginary part of the RPA polarizability's second derivative. By redefining this expression, we found that dividing the imaginary part of the RPA polarizability's second derivative by a factor of -1 yields the Jost function, which is utilized to determine the RPA eigenenergies and widths. Calculating the Jost function for various energies allows us to identify the position, width, and residual interaction-induced width of $^{16}$O's 44.72 MeV electric giant dipole resonance.
