This paper introduces a novel generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), an enhanced WaveNet model that generates raw audio waveforms. By integrating pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks, QPNet effectively captures both short-term and long-term periodic patterns within audio signals. This allows QPNet to generate longer sequences of high-quality audio than the original WaveNet model. Our research demonstrates that QPNet surpasses WaveNet in terms of sequence generation length and audio quality, while also reducing the training time. Furthermore, QPNet achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art transformer-based raw audio generators, but with a more compact model size.

This research introduces MADARi, an online platform for the annotation and
correction of Modern Standard Arabic texts, specifically aimed at addressing
morphological ambiguities. The interface allows users to mark up and correct
words within a text, including their base form, part of speech, and possible
translations. Additionally, the platform includes a spell-checking feature
that suggests corrections for misspelled words. Users can access and manage
their annotations through a personal account, with options to export marked-up
text in various formats.

The atmospheres of temperate gas-rich exoplanets, which are thought to be similar to those of Earth, are not well understood due to the limited availability of suitable targets. By analyzing the effects of atmospheric chemistry on temperate gas-rich exoplanets, we aim to provide a comprehensive framework for interpreting the results of future spectroscopic studies. We utilize a 1D radiative-convective model to simulate the atmospheres of three temperate gas-rich exoplanets, including Kepler-167e, Kepler-452b, and Gliese 832c, and then employ a chemical equilibrium model to determine the abundance of various species. Our analysis reveals that the atmospheres of these planets are primarily composed of hydrogen, helium, water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, ammonia, and sulfur gases. We also examine the potential for atmospheric escape and find that it has a significant impact on the abundance of certain species, particularly in the case of Kepler-452b. By considering the effects of stellar X-rays and extreme ultraviolet radiation, we find that they can lead to the formation of oxygen atoms and molecules, as well as water vapor, in the upper atmospheres of these planets. Our analysis also reveals that the atmospheres of these planets can be distinguished through spectroscopic observations in the near-infrared and visible regions of the electromagnetic spectrum.

To verify the existence of Majorana fermions, we propose a tunneling spectroscopy method that involves using resistive electrodes to measure tunneling conductance. By accounting for ohmic losses, we can differentiate the signature of a Majorana peak from other peaks that may arise during measurements. The Majorana peak is characterized by a specific, symmetrical pattern of conductance fluctuations as the phase difference between the tunneling electrodes changes. In contrast, other peaks exhibit asymmetrical conductance fluctuations that vary in response to changes in the tunneling voltage and temperature. Our method also enables the calculation of the Majorana gap energy by analyzing the tunneling voltage dependence of the conductance at specific points, and we demonstrate that this approach is robust against various sources of noise.

The development of advanced detection algorithms through deep learning has accelerated the identification of road issues, including automatic detection of defects and markings. However, the current implementation of these techniques in a comprehensive management system is hindered by the lack of a unified platform that can seamlessly integrate detection tools, data management solutions, and interactive visualization capabilities. To address this limitation, we present RoadAtlas, a cutting-edge platform that enables the efficient detection of road flaws and markings, as well as effective data management and visualization. Built on a modular architecture, RoadAtlas incorporates a range of advanced detection algorithms, data storage solutions, and interactive tools to facilitate seamless data processing, storage, and analysis.

We establish a connection between shadows from the theory of bicategories and the concept of traces in monoidal categories. By drawing from Atiyah axioms and applying them in a bicategorical context, we derive a definition for extended shadows in monoidal 2-categories. It is then shown that shadows are equivalent to traces when restricted to symmetric monoidal categories. Additionally, we explore how this relationship between shadows and traces is maintained across different levels of categorification.

We're investigating a challenging sound localization issue - pinpointing visual sounds in video based on associated images. Our goal is to develop a method that can locate sounds in videos by analyzing corresponding images and video frames. To achieve this, we propose a technique that uses a sound source generator model to predict the sound's origin from the image, and then refines this prediction using a video-based model that takes into account the sound's propagation. Our approach is to train the generator model on a dataset that includes images with embedded sounds and their corresponding audio recordings. We then use this model to generate a 3D map of the sound's origin from the image, and combine it with a video-based model that uses the sound's propagation to refine the prediction. Our results show that our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art technique, particularly for sounds originating from the sides.

Recent studies have shown that Euclidean graph convolutional networks can be reformulated using the first-order approximation of reparameterization techniques. However, these methods are limited to Euclidean spaces and cannot be directly applied to Lorentzian spaces, which are essential for modeling directed edges in networks. To address this limitation, we propose a new framework for Lorentzian graph convolutional networks, providing a flexible and customizable framework for various network reparameterization methods. Our approach is based on a novel, general reparameterization trick that can be applied to different parameterizations, including mean-field and non-mean-field types. By leveraging this approach, we derive a unified optimization objective for our proposed Lorentzian graph convolutional networks, demonstrating its efficiency and effectiveness through comprehensive experiments and comparisons on multiple benchmark datasets.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem to identify unknown parameters within a structural acoustic interaction model, composed of a rigid boundary separating two acoustic fluids and an elastic plate. We are given incomplete and noisy data resulting from the movement of one fluid, and our objective is to recover the elastic plate's parameters. A unique solution exists for this inverse problem, and we utilize the Tikhonov regularization method to find it numerically, demonstrating our approach with a graphical example.

A new method has been developed to generate steady-state squeezing in optomechanical systems, allowing for the amplification of an input signal reflected back from a mechanical oscillator. This technique involves using a cavity connected to an oscillator and fed with a coherent light, and involves a unique interaction between the light and mechanical components. By analyzing this interaction, it becomes possible to measure key parameters, such as the mechanical quality factor and the strength of the optomechanical interaction. The method can also be modified to produce squeezed vacuum states, and the developed optomechanical model can be applied to study the effects of different environmental conditions on its performance.

We've modified the modal mu-calculus to incorporate atomically structured trees, introducing both scalar and vectorial operators under the name mu^{\oplus}_{\sim}\phi, where \oplus can be either union (denoted as \vee) or intersection (denoted as \wedge), and \sim represents either negation (\sim) or preservation (\sim). Our analysis focuses on the complexity of the number of atoms required for a formula to express a given property, resulting in an NPT-complete language when using disunion operators, whereas the use of conjunction leads to an NPT-hard but decidable fragment.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model that modifies the
standard exponential model to account for the effects of impulsivity and
self-control, using the Tsallis exponential function. This new model retains
the simplicity of the original exponential model while capturing the observed
asymmetries in delay discounting behavior. We demonstrate that the Tsallis
exponential model's parameters can be interpreted as impulsivity and self-control
components, and we provide a new framework for understanding the relationship
between impulsivity and delay discounting. Additionally, we show that the
Tsallis exponential model can be reduced to several well-known delay discounting
models, including the standard exponential model, the hyperbolic model, and the
logarithmic model, depending on specific conditions.

In this note, we explore a new harmonic gauge condition that can be applied to the massive gravity theory's auxiliary field. By adopting this new gauge, we find that the auxiliary field's equation of motion is simplified, and it takes the same form as the de Rham-Goldstone mode's equation of motion. This new gauge also facilitates the comparison between the massive gravity theory and the bimetric theory, allowing us to derive the same equations of motion for the modes as those found in the bimetric theory when a specific symmetry is imposed.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs has been the focus of various studies in the field of graph theory. Recently, researchers have been particularly interested in the properties of a specific type of signed graph known as extended double covers (EDCs) of graphs. In this study, we aim to investigate the relationship between the number of EDCs of a given graph and another graph, specifically examining how this number is affected by different variables such as the size and the properties of the graph in question. We have established upper and lower bounds for the number of EDCs of a graph, and we have also explored how these bounds can be achieved through various homomorphism mappings between different graphs.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, we've developed an invariant, Weyl-Wigner form of the canonical density matrix using a phase-space representation, which can be seen as a real and symmetric transformation of the usual Pauli and Stratonovich representation. This new form of the density matrix allows us to derive an explicit formula for its coherent states and an algebraic proof of the quantum de Finetti theorem.

The concept of negative absolute temperature has been misinterpreted as it's often seen as a far-fetched idea. In reality, negative temperature refers to a specific condition in statistics and thermodynamics, indicating a situation where the majority of a system's members have higher energy compared to a normal distribution. This notion has been applied to various contexts, including the analysis of spin systems and laser-light interactions. Notably, the Sagnac effect demonstrates that negative temperature can be achieved and has practical implications. It's essential to address the misconceptions surrounding negative absolute temperature and to provide a clear definition of this concept.

Let G be an abelian group and A a nonempty subset of G, with elements indexed as $a_0, a_1,..., a_{k-1}$. For any positive integer h less than or equal to k, we define the h-restricted signed sumset of A as $h\SS_{\pm}(A) = \{\sum_{i=0}^{h-1} (\pm a_i) : 0 \leq h \leq k\}$. In this paper, we provide upper and lower bounds for the number of elements in $h\SS_{\pm}(A)$, specifically $|h\SS_{\pm}(A)| \geq |A|^{h-1}$ and $|h\SS_{\pm}(A)| \leq |A|^h$. Additionally, given a prime p, we establish a lower bound for the number of elements in $h\SS_{\pm}(A)$ modulo p, specifically $|h\SS_{\pm}(A) \mod p| \geq |A|^{h-1}$ when $|A| \geq p$.

A new dataset called UniToPatho has been created to aid in the development of computer systems that can automatically diagnose colorectal polyps from histological samples. This dataset comprises 1,000 high-resolution images of colorectal polyps, along with a severity grading from mild to severe dysplasia. The images were obtained from 100 different patients and annotated by experienced pathologists. To ensure the accuracy of these annotations, a secondary review was conducted by a panel of three pathologists. The UniToPatho dataset includes annotations for three tasks: polyp classification, and two levels of adenoma grading. The dataset is unique in its large size and detailed annotations, making it suitable for training and testing advanced computer systems that can classify and grade colorectal polyps based on histological samples.

A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering problems involving smoothly varying material properties and complex geometric obstacles. This method combines a recent adaptive technique for solving boundary-value problems with the use of high-order finite elements, allowing for optimal mesh refinement based on the frequency and problem characteristics. A priori and a posteriori estimates have been established to ensure the accuracy of the solutions, and the results show that the proposed method can achieve highly precise results even at high frequencies.

Water in the form of hydroxyl within the crystals of pyroxene from the Chelyabinsk and Benenitra meteorites has been re-examined.  The analysis of these samples indicates that the water content is significantly higher than previously reported, with an estimated 0.2-0.3 weight percent of water within the pyroxene from the Chelyabinsk meteorite and 0.1-0.2 weight percent from the Benenitra meteorite.  This water is not the result of terrestrial contamination, as demonstrated by the lack of water within the pyroxene from the same meteorites that has been thermally altered to form glass.  The water within the pyroxene is also not the result of solar nebula, as it is not present within the thermally altered glass.  Instead, it is proposed that the water within the pyroxene is the result of the interaction between the hot surface of the young Sun and the inner solar system, specifically within the region where the orbits of Mercury and Venus lie.  This water would have been incorporated into the pyroxene through the process of metamorphism that occurred as a result of the heating of the surface of the planetesimals.  This evidence supports the idea that the delivery of water to the early Earth occurred through the process of impacts from planetesimals that had been heated and altered by the young Sun.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find explicit expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ chains. This includes both finite and infinite chains, as well as integrable t-J models related to these chains. We demonstrate that the quantum-group symmetry of these models can be represented through a set of conserved operators, which are linked to the R-matrix and the symmetry algebra. This representation enables us to derive explicit expressions for scalar products and form factors, which can be applied to obtain a wide range of results, including correlation functions and response functions for these models.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Presently, most approaches to this task require significant training data and human intervention. This research seeks to break this mold by introducing a novel technique that enables speech-to-text translation without any need for training data in the target language. This method utilizes a novel neural network that can learn to translate spoken language into written language without any need for training data in the target language. This neural network is trained on spoken language-to-spoken language pairs and written language-to-written language pairs for the same languages. This model can then be adapted to translate spoken language into written language for new language pairs. This technique is tested on speech-to-text datasets for English to French and English to German, yielding impressive results.

We have derived a comprehensive set of multipolar expansions suitable for
simulating interactions between complex nanostructures and external electromagnetic fields. These expressions can be applied to a broad range of situations, from which we have specifically examined the formulations for electromagnetic fields and optical force calculations. By combining these descriptions, we have developed a comprehensive framework for evaluating optical forces on multi-component particles and nanostructures. This framework is particularly valuable as it can provide accurate results even when the size of the particles is comparable to the wavelength of light.

This research extends the concept of quantum immanants to a broader context, incorporating double Young-Capelli bitableaux and Schur shifted symmetric functions. We demonstrate that these more general immanants are equivalent to a specific class of Schur positive elements, which includes the Schur expanded versions of shifted Schur polynomials. Furthermore, we derive a formula to compute the coefficients of these Schur functions using a product of two elementary symmetric functions, expressed in terms of the contents of specific Young diagrams. This formula allows us to express the shifted Schur functions as a sum of monomials, which can be viewed as a generalization of the classical "hook formula".

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we investigate the implications of adding a minimal dark matter sector consisting of one WIMP state. By incorporating the most fundamental scalar doublets required for neutrino oscillations, we can break the lepton number symmetry while generating the small neutrino masses. Additionally, the most basic BL$\in$R symmetry breaking mechanism can provide the necessary mass scales for the zeroth-order fields. By examining the most fundamental approach to the most basic scoto-seesaw model, we can determine the constraints on the parameter space that satisfy the requirements for the WIMP dark matter state to function effectively. Furthermore, we investigate the stability of the Higgs vacuum by analyzing the most fundamental approach to the most basic scoto-seesaw model, including the impact of the most basic scalar doublets and BL$\in$R symmetry breaking on the Higgs vacuum stability.

A crucial factor in the physics of transition metal oxides is the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states of the 3$d$ and 4$d$ transition metals. However, the extent of this mixing has not been thoroughly examined for 5$d$ electrons despite its significance. Utilizing a 5$d$ electron model with a strong on-site Coulomb interaction, we investigated the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals in both 4$d$ and 5$d$ transition metal oxides. Our analysis reveals that the mixing of these orbitals is more pronounced in 5$d$ than in 4$d$ electrons. This increased mixing in 5$d$ electrons is attributed to the larger crystal field splitting in 5$d$ oxides, which results in a more significant overlap between the $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals. Consequently, the mixing of these orbitals has a substantial impact on the physics of 5$d$ transition metal oxides, particularly in the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling.

This research investigates how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it examines the behavior of relative quantum cohomology as it relates to symplectic symmetries and Kähler metrics in complex geometric spaces undergoing these transformations.

A computer vision technique called image editing has the potential to enhance
medical imaging for various purposes, including improving the accuracy of
artificial intelligence models used in disease diagnosis. In this study, we focus
on chest X-rays and aim to develop an algorithm that can realistically alter
abnormal images to depict healthy lungs. We call this task "disease-aware image
deletion" and have already established a baseline method involving an adversarial
network. To train and evaluate our algorithm, we created a dataset of 1000
chest X-rays with corresponding masks highlighting the lung area. These images
were labeled as either normal or containing one of five lung conditions:
pneumonia, heart failure, lung cancer, pleural effusion, or a collapsed lung.
Our initial results showed that a simple deletion algorithm was able to remove
the disease from the lung area with some success, but the edited images were
not visually similar to actual healthy lung images.

ViDaExpert is a tool designed for the interactive visualization and advanced
analysis of high-dimensional vectorial data, including its nonlinear extension.
It enables users to explore multi-dimensional spaces by projecting data onto
lower-dimensional spaces, and offers a range of tools for in-depth analysis.
ViDaExpert allows for the identification of clusters, calculation of
neighborhoods, determination of data density and outliers, and more.
Developed for the visualization of vectorial data resulting from diffusion
tensor imaging, ViDaExpert is a versatile tool that can be used for the
examination of diffusion tensor data and its derivatives, including Q-ball
imaging, mean k-apparent diffusion coefficient (KADC) imaging, and others.
ViDaExpert is a user-friendly tool that can be used for the visualization of
any high-dimensional vectorial data, and is available for download at
https://github.com/stephane-ouellet/vidaexpert.

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for various applications including computational physics, engineering, and data analysis. When dealing with irregular domains, a common approach involves dividing the boundary into smaller segments and computing the potential as a sum of local contributions. A new, more effective method for this calculation has been developed. By expressing the potential as a combination of elementary functions, such as logarithms and arctan, the algorithm significantly reduces the computational cost compared to traditional methods. This new approach is particularly beneficial when the domain contains many closely spaced boundary points, as it minimizes errors associated with polynomial approximations. A specific implementation of this method is presented, along with its application to solving the Laplace equation using a boundary integral formulation. This implementation is shown to outperform existing methods in terms of performance and accuracy, as demonstrated on several examples.
